subject: Animation
title: Émile Reynaud's Praxinoscope
description: A 60-second lesson on Émile Reynaud's Praxinoscope.

hook.text: In 1877, Émile Reynaud replaced the zoetrope's slits with a ring of mirrors inside the drum.

buildup.text: The mirrors reflected each drawing in sequence, producing a brighter and sharper moving image.

discovery.text: Reynaud then built his Théâtre Optique and projected animated stories for paying audiences.

twist.text: His shows ran at a Paris museum for five years, a decade before the Lumière brothers' cinema.

climax.text: Audiences watched hand-painted characters move on screen, the first projected animation ever.

punchline.text: Reynaud screened animation before cinema existed.

quiz.question: What did Reynaud add to improve the zoetrope?
options: A ring of mirrors replacing the slits

details.summary: Émile Reynaud improved on the zoetrope with his praxinoscope in 1877, then created the Théâtre Optique to project animated stories for paying audiences years before cinema. His Pantomimes Lumineuses of 1892 were the world's first public animation screenings.
details.whyItMatters: Reynaud staged the first public animation shows three years before the Lumière brothers projected their first film. His forgotten achievement establishes that animation preceded cinema, not the reverse.
takeaways: Reynaud's praxinoscope used mirrors to improve on the zoetrope's viewing quality
His 1892 Théâtre Optique shows were the first public animation screenings
Animation was publicly exhibited before cinema itself existed

faq.question: How did Reynaud's Théâtre Optique work?
faq.answer: Reynaud painted hundreds of images on flexible strips, projected them through a system of mirrors and lenses onto a screen, and manually controlled the speed and direction. He could run sequences forward, backward, and pause — primitive but effective interactive animation projection.

faq.question: Why is Reynaud largely forgotten despite his pioneering work?
faq.answer: Cinema overwhelmed his hand-painted projection system. Devastated by obsolescence, Reynaud reportedly destroyed his machines and threw his painted strips into the Seine. Without preserved work, his revolutionary contribution faded from popular memory.
